overview.intro: Economics begins with scarcity: human wants are unlimited while the means to satisfy them are limited, and every society must therefore choose. This unit builds the foundations. It traces the definition of economics from Adam Smith’s wealth-focused definition through the welfare and growth definitions to Samuelson’s growth-and-allocation definition, separates microeconomics from macroeconomics, establishes the basic concepts of utility, value, wealth and welfare, sets out the three problems every economy must solve, and compares the capitalist, socialist and mixed systems that different societies have chosen to solve them.

learn.title: Definitions of economics: Smith to Samuelson

blocks.text: Adam Smith, in 1776, defined economics as the science of wealth, arguing that the study of how nations produce and accumulate wealth explains their prosperity. Critics objected that the definition made money the end of life rather than the means, and Thomas Carlyle called economics the dismal science for precisely that reason. Alfred Marshall answered in 1890 by placing man at the centre: economics is a study of mankind in the ordinary business of life, examining the individual and social actions most closely connected with the attainment and use of the material requisites of wellbeing, wealth being treated as a means to the end of welfare rather than an end in itself.

Lionel Robbins attacked both by defining economics in terms of scarcity in 1932: it is the science which studies human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means which have alternative uses. The three elements of the definition are unlimited ends, scarce means, and the fact that the scarce means have alternative uses, which is what makes choice unavoidable. The criticism of Robbins is that he excluded welfare and growth altogether, and Paul Samuelson combined the strands into a definition covering both the allocation of scarce resources to competing ends and the growth of those resources over time.

blocks.text: Microeconomics studies the individual units of the economy: a household, a firm, the price of a particular commodity and the market for it. It asks how a consumer allocates income among goods, how a firm sets output to maximise profit, and how a price is determined in one market. Macroeconomics studies the aggregates: national income, total output, the general price level, employment, and the balance of payments. The two are inseparable, because aggregate outcomes are the sum of individual decisions while individual decisions respond to aggregate conditions such as the interest rate.

blocks.caption: Microeconomics against macroeconomics

items: Micro assumes the aggregate background is given and studies one market at a time.
Macro treats the economy as one aggregate and studies the interrelations between aggregates.
A fall in one price may be micro; a rise in the general price level is macro.
The two must be read together: individual choices build the aggregate, aggregates redirect the individual.

blocks.text: Utility is the capacity of a good to satisfy a want, and it is the basis of demand. Total utility is the sum of satisfaction from all units consumed, while marginal utility is the additional satisfaction from one more unit, and it declines as consumption increases. Value has two senses: value in use, which is the utility of a thing, and value in exchange, which is the amount of other things for which it can be traded. Adam Smith’s paradox of value observes that water has enormous use value but low exchange value, while diamonds have little use value but high exchange value, and the resolution lies in scarcity and marginal utility rather than in total usefulness.

blocks.text: Wealth in economics means a stock of valuable assets that yield income, and an item qualifies only if it is scarce, transferable, possessable and productive of income. Welfare is broader than wealth: it includes health, leisure and freedom, which is why an economy can grow in output while wellbeing stagnates.

learn.title: The basic problems and the three economic systems

blocks.text: Every economy, however rich or poor, must answer three questions. What to produce decides which goods and in what quantities are made, which is a choice between consumer and capital goods and between luxury and necessity. How to produce decides the technique, capital-intensive where labour is expensive and scarce, labour-intensive where labour is plentiful and cheap. For whom to produce decides the distribution of output among the members of society, and it is answered by the reward each factor receives.

The three systems differ in who gives those answers. A capitalist economy answers them through the price mechanism: consumer demand signals what to produce, factor prices guide how to produce, and the distribution of factor earnings settles for whom. A socialist economy answers them through a central planning authority, which fixes the targets and the allocation. A mixed economy retains the private sector for most decisions while the state owns and directs key industries and provides public goods.

keyPoints: Economics arises from scarcity: unlimited wants against limited means.
Smith defined it as the science of wealth; Marshall as a study of human welfare.
Robbins defined it as choice between ends using scarce means with alternative uses.
Samuelson combines allocation with the growth of resources.
Microeconomics studies individual units; macroeconomics studies aggregates.
Utility is want-satisfying capacity; marginal utility declines as consumption rises.
Value in use and value in exchange differ, which explains the paradox of value.
Wealth is a stock of income-producing assets; welfare is broader than wealth.
The three basic problems are what to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce.
Capitalism answers them through price, socialism through planning, mixed economies through both.
examFocus: Definition questions should give the economist, the emphasis and the criticism of each, since marks are for the progression rather than one sentence.
Micro and macro comparisons are best answered in a table taking one basis at a time.
System questions should be answered against the three basic problems, which is the organising idea of the unit.

questions.prompt: The definition of economics that emphasises scarcity and choice is associated with:
questions.explanation: Robbins defined economics as the study of choice between ends using scarce means that have alternative uses.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a subject matter of microeconomics rather than macroeconomics?
options: The wage rate in one industry
The fiscal deficit of the country
questions.answer: The wage rate in one industry
questions.explanation: A single market or industry price is a microeconomic question, while the rest are aggregates of the whole economy.

questions.prompt: The paradox of value, that water is cheap yet diamonds are dear, is explained by:
options: Total utility of water being low
Marginal utility and scarcity rather than total usefulness
questions.answer: Marginal utility and scarcity rather than total usefulness
questions.explanation: What determines exchange value is the marginal utility of the available unit and its scarcity, not the total usefulness of the good.

questions.prompt: In a socialist economy the three basic problems are answered by:
options: The price mechanism in a free market
The interaction of demand and supply in each market
questions.explanation: A socialist system allocates resources by plan rather than by price, so the planning board decides what, how and for whom to produce.

questions.prompt: The additional satisfaction obtained from consuming one more unit of a good is called __________ utility.
questions.explanation: Marginal utility normally declines as consumption increases, which is the reason a demand curve slopes downward.

questions.prompt: The study of individual units such as a household, a firm or a single market is known as __________ economics.
questions.explanation: Microeconomics takes the aggregate background as given and studies one unit or market at a time, while macroeconomics studies the aggregates themselves.

questions.prompt: State the three basic problems of every economy and explain any one of them.
questions.answer: The three problems are what to produce, which goods and in what quantities; how to produce, which technique of production to use; and for whom to produce, how the output is distributed among the people. What to produce is a choice between consumer and capital goods and between necessities and luxuries, made necessary because resources are limited while wants are unlimited, and answered in a market economy by consumer demand expressed through price.
questions.explanation: All three must be named and one explained, since naming alone earns only part of the marks.

questions.prompt: Distinguish microeconomics from macroeconomics on three bases.
questions.answer: On the unit of study, microeconomics examines individual units such as a household, a firm or a single market, while macroeconomics examines aggregates such as national income, employment and the general price level. On the central question, micro asks how a particular price or output is determined, while macro asks how the overall level of income and prices is determined. On application, micro supports price regulation and competition policy, while macro supports monetary and fiscal policy. The method also differs, micro using price theory and macro using income and employment theory.
questions.explanation: Three bases of comparison are required, each stated as a contrast between the two fields.

questions.prompt: Explain the four definitions of economics in order and state how each was criticised.
questions.answer: Adam Smith in 1776 defined economics as the science of wealth, studying how nations produce and accumulate wealth, and was criticised for making wealth the end of life rather than a means. Alfred Marshall in 1890 placed man at the centre, defining economics as the study of mankind in the ordinary business of life in relation to material requisites of wellbeing, but was criticised for overstating material welfare and neglecting non-material wellbeing. Lionel Robbins in 1932 defined it as the study of choice between unlimited ends and scarce means having alternative uses, which gave rigour but excluded welfare and gave no account of growth. Samuelson then combined the two strands, defining economics in terms of both the growth of output and the efficient allocation of scarce resources among competing ends, which answers the earlier criticisms by covering choice, welfare and growth together.
questions.explanation: Full marks need the sequence, the emphasis of each definition and the criticism that drove the next one.

questions.prompt: A government decides to stop subsidising fertiliser in order to fund rural schools. Classify the decision under the three basic problems, identify whether it is a micro or macro measure, and say how each of the three systems would approach it.
questions.answer: The decision answers what to produce: resources are being shifted from a farm input to a social service, which is a choice between two uses of the same budget. It answers how to produce indirectly, since cheaper fertiliser encouraged a chemical-intensive technique and its removal changes the incentive to use labour and organic methods. It answers for whom to produce, because the benefit moves from farmers receiving a subsidy to rural children receiving schooling. As a policy it is macro in intent, since it reallocates a national budget and affects agricultural output and literacy aggregates, though its effect on one input market is micro. In a capitalist system the market would have set the fertiliser price and the state would fund schools from general taxation; in a socialist system the planning board would have fixed both the fertiliser allocation and school construction directly; in a mixed economy, which is India’s choice, the state withdraws from one price decision and enters another, using the price mechanism deliberately for a social end.
questions.explanation: The answer earns marks for handling all three problems, for distinguishing the level of the measure, and for applying each system rather than describing them in the abstract.
